name: Syrian Steppe and Palmyra
blurb: Wormwood steppe, bedouin flocks, lizards and raptors around the Palmyra oasis.

tip.title: Overgraze the steppe
tip.text: Flocks of sheep and goats now do most of the grazing. Raise Domestic sheep and goats by 100% and watch the shrubs and grasses, then the jirds, lizards and raptors that live among them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Winter rain
nodes.desc: Little rain falls on the steppe, mostly in the cooler months, and it decides how much plant growth the year gets. What does fall drains toward salt flats.

nodes.name: Oasis springs and wadi
nodes.desc: Springs such as Efqa and the small al-Qubur wadi water the Palmyra oasis, which supports palms and gardens amid dry desert.

nodes.name: Stony, salty soils
nodes.desc: The plateau is limestone with chert gravel, and run-off ends in salt flats. Poor soil and little water limit plant cover.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, dung and carcasses, returning nutrients to the thin desert soil.

nodes.name: White wormwood
nodes.desc: A low grey shrub of dry steppe and a main climax plant of the Syrian Desert. It is good fodder, mainly for sheep.

nodes.name: Shrubby saltbush
nodes.desc: A salt-tolerant shrub, named as a climax plant of the Syrian steppe, and a mainstay of grazing land.

nodes.name: Feather grass
nodes.desc: A tussock grass named among the climax plants of the Syrian Desert. Overgrazing has replaced such plants with grasses of lower feed value.

nodes.name: Date palm
nodes.desc: Palms grow in the spring-fed oasis of Palmyra, one of the few reliably watered patches in the surrounding desert.

nodes.name: Domestic sheep and goats
nodes.desc: Bedouin flocks of sheep and goats are now the main grazers of the Syrian Desert, and heavy grazing has degraded the rangeland.

nodes.name: Tristram's jird
nodes.desc: A gerbil-like rodent of dry open ground in the Levant, which feeds on seeds and plant matter. It is common prey for raptors.

nodes.name: Asia Minor ground squirrel
nodes.desc: A burrowing ground squirrel of open steppe that eats plants and is taken by buzzards and kestrels.

nodes.name: Pitted darkling beetle
nodes.desc: A large ground beetle of the desert that feeds on plant debris. Darkling beetles are a staple food of the bald ibis.

nodes.name: Crested lark
nodes.desc: A common ground-feeding bird of open steppe that eats seeds and insects. It is among the most recorded birds here.

nodes.name: Bosc's fringe-toed lizard
nodes.desc: A fast, insect-eating lizard of sandy and gravelly ground. Lizards are a major food for birds and snakes here.

nodes.name: Long-eared hedgehog
nodes.desc: A small desert hedgehog that hunts at night for beetles and other invertebrates, and also takes small lizards.

nodes.name: Large whip snake
nodes.desc: A fast diurnal snake that hunts lizards, rodents and birds in open and rocky country.

nodes.name: Northern bald ibis
nodes.desc: Rediscovered near Palmyra in 2002. It probes the steppe for lizards and darkling beetles. The colony has since died out.

nodes.name: Eurasian kestrel
nodes.desc: A small falcon that hovers over open ground and takes rodents, lizards, small birds and insects.

nodes.name: Little owl
nodes.desc: A small owl of open dry country that hunts small birds, rodents and insects, often at dusk.

nodes.name: Egyptian vulture
nodes.desc: A small vulture that eats mainly carrion, such as dead livestock, along with dung, insects and eggs.

nodes.name: Long-legged buzzard
nodes.desc: A steppe buzzard that takes mainly rodents and ground squirrels, plus many reptiles, birds and insects.
